Chapter 4: Undermining International Law and Global Institutions
Imagine this: In a bustling city, there’s a law student hunched over her desk, surrounded by heavy casebooks about the United Nations and all the rules that are supposed to keep countries in check. She’s genuinely drawn to the idea that nations can actually solve tough problems peacefully—through conversation and compromise, not threats or force.
But the more she reads, the more she spots something troubling. The rules? They’re often twisted, or just flat-out ignored—especially by the countries holding the most power.
Now, let’s talk about the United States. With its vast resources and global influence, America’s played a huge role in shaping how the world works together. But here’s the catch: whenever international law gets in the way of its goals, the U.S. often just... makes its own path. Treaties are signed, then dropped. Agreements are made, then broken. The unspoken message? The rules are for everyone else—not for those who set them.
One example really sticks with our law student. Not long ago, the United Nations Security Council refused to approve military action in a major conflict. But the U.S. and its allies pushed ahead anyway, insisting their cause was just. That decision set off outrage around the globe. Other nations saw it as a dangerously slippery slope. After all, if the world’s most powerful country can ignore the rules, what’s to stop anyone else from doing the same?
And this isn’t just a recent issue—it’s been happening for decades. Throughout the postwar era, the U.S. has used its influence to steer the international system in its favor. When global institutions line up with American interests, they get praise and funding. But the moment they push back, they’re brushed aside as irrelevant or even obstructive.
The end result? We’ve got a world order that’s both strong and fragile. Sure, it can accomplish amazing things, but it’s also vulnerable—especially when those with the most power decide to change the rules on a whim.
Now, think about what this means for smaller countries. Without the protection of international law, they’re left to fend for themselves, navigating a world where might often wins out over what’s right. All those efforts to build a more just and fair global system? They get undermined by the reality of power politics. The whole idea of collective security starts to sound a little empty when the rules themselves can shift overnight.
So, as our law student looks back on everything she’s learned, she can’t help but wonder—what would it actually take to create a system where every nation truly stands equal before the law? She dreams of a world where cooperation and respect replace the old logic of dominance.
But as long as the most powerful countries reserve the right to go it alone, that dream of a fair and peaceful international order stays just out of reach.
